Introduction to sdmhelpers

Source: vignettes/introduction.Rmd
introduction.Rmd

Overview

sdmhelpers provides helper functions for species distribution modelling (SDM) workflows, with particular emphasis on presence-background models implemented with maxnet. The package contains tools for constructing sampling-bias surfaces from target-group records, weighting target-group observations by seasonal or combined seasonal and diel overlap, selecting complete spatial folds for independent testing, screening environmental predictors, and evaluating predictions using the True Skill Statistic (TSS).

Presence-only SDMs are sensitive to differences between the sampling process that generated species observations and the process used to select background locations. A commonly used approach is therefore to select or weight background data so that they reflect similar sampling bias to the presence data (Phillips et al. 2009; Elith et al. 2011). sdmhelpers extends this idea by allowing records from a target group to contribute unequally according to their temporal similarity to the focal species.

The examples below use datasets distributed with sdmhelpers. They are reduced or pseudonymised datasets intended for demonstrating package functionality, not for biological inference.

sdmhelpers was developed as part of the project HiQBioDiv: High-resolution quantification of biodiversity for conservation and management, funded by the Latvian Council of Science (Ref. No. VPP-VARAM-DABA-2024/1-0002).

The development version can be installed from GitHub with:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("aavotins/sdmhelpers")

Packages used in this vignette:

library(sdmhelpers)
library(sf)
#> Linking to GEOS 3.12.1, GDAL 3.8.4, PROJ 9.4.0; sf_use_s2() is TRUE
library(ggplot2)
library(terra)
#> terra 1.9.50
library(maxnet)
library(SDMtune)

Example data

Several example datasets are included in the package. The examples in this vignette use bird and bryophyte observations, spatial presence and background locations, spatial blocks, a 100-m grid, known habitat-inventory dates, and an example environmental raster.

data("aves_small", package = "sdmhelpers")
data("bryophyta_one", package = "sdmhelpers")
data("habitat_inventories", package = "sdmhelpers")
data("points100", package = "sdmhelpers")
data("example_grid", package = "sdmhelpers")
example_grid <- terra::unwrap(example_grid)
data("example_presences", package = "sdmhelpers")
data("example_background", package = "sdmhelpers")
data("example_independent_blocks", package = "sdmhelpers")
data("egv_names", package = "sdmhelpers")

The environmental raster used later in the vignette is stored in inst/extdata.

egv_file <- system.file("extdata",
                        "example_egv.tif",
                        package = "sdmhelpers")

Simple target-group bias surface

Target-group background sampling uses observations of taxa that are expected to have been collected through a sampling process similar to that of the focal species. If sampling effort is spatially biased, drawing background data from the same biased sampling domain can reduce the contrast between presence and background sampling processes (Phillips et al. 2009).

Here, one species from aves_small is treated as the focal species while all species form the target group. For this example, the focal species is chosen programmatically as the species with the largest number of records so that the example does not depend on a particular species name.

target_species <- names(
  sort(table(aves_small$species), decreasing = TRUE)
)[1]

target_species
#> [1] "Strix aluco"

target_group <- aves_small

Multiple observations can occur in the same 100-m grid cell. For the spatial bias surface, records are therefore counted by grid cell and supplied to kde_surface() as weights.

tg_counts <- aggregate(
  list(n_records = rep(1, nrow(target_group))),
  by = list(id100 = target_group$id100),
  FUN = sum
)

idx <- match(tg_counts$id100, points100$id)
keep <- !is.na(idx)

tg_points <- points100[idx[keep], ]
tg_points$n_records <- tg_counts$n_records[keep]

tg_points
#> Simple feature collection with 1065 features and 7 fields

#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 459750 ymin: 285250 xmax: 519650 ymax: 329550

#> First 10 features:
#>                     id yes tks50km rinda300       ID1km rinda500
#> 1714235 100mX4597Y3042   1    4221   385184 1kmX459Y304   236094

#> 1719476 100mX4604Y3043   1    4221   386592 1kmX460Y304   236096

#> 1723202 100mX4609Y3038   1    4221   383781 1kmX460Y303   235197
#> 1723204 100mX4609Y3040   1    4221   385188 1kmX460Y304   236097
#> 1723921 100mX4610Y3013   1    4221   372533 1kmX461Y301   230697
#> 1723922 100mX4610Y3014   1    4221   372533 1kmX461Y301   231597
#> 1723926 100mX4610Y3018   1    4221   373936 1kmX461Y301   231597
#> 1723950 100mX4610Y3042   1    4221   385189 1kmX461Y304   236097
#>                          geom n_records
#> 1714235 POINT (459750 304250)         1
#> 1714987 POINT (459850 304450)         1

#> 1723926 POINT (461050 301850)         2
#> 1723950 POINT (461050 304250)         1

kde_surface() first bins point weights to the reference raster and then applies Gaussian smoothing. This makes the calculation practical for large rasters and large bandwidths. Kernel density estimation in general is described by Silverman (1986).

The example grid uses EPSG:3059, whose map units are metres, so sigma = 3000 corresponds to a Gaussian bandwidth of 3 km. With normalize = "pdf", the resulting surface is normalised to integrate to one and represents a probability-density-scaled surface of the spatial distribution of target-group records. It can therefore be used as a relative proxy sampling-bias surface for background sampling.

simple_bias <- kde_surface(
  x = tg_points,
  weight_field = "n_records",
  sigma = 3000,
  ref = example_grid,
  normalize = "pdf",
  mask = TRUE
)

options(scipen = 999)
terra::plot(simple_bias, main = "Simple target-group bias")

Unweighted target-group sampling-bias surface.

This simple approach assumes that every target-group record is equally informative about the sampling process affecting the focal species. The following sections relax that assumption.

Phenologically weighted target-group

Species observed by the same people or recording scheme may nevertheless have different seasonal detectability, availability, or both. A species recorded mainly in winter, for example, may provide little information about sampling effort relevant to a species recorded mainly during late spring.

phenology_overlap_weights() estimates overlap between species’ day-of-year distributions using overlapping::overlap() (Pastore and Calcagnì 2019). This approach provides compatibility with conventional kernel-density overlap estimation (Pastore 2018). However, because day of year is treated as a linear variable, observations near the end and beginning of the calendar year are not considered adjacent. For species with observation periods spanning this boundary, torus_overlap_many() provides an alternative based on circular kernel-density estimation with constant (e.g. midday) value for the time of day.

First, day of year is added to the bird records.

bird_dates <- aves_small
bird_dates$DoY <- as.POSIXlt(bird_dates$date)$yday + 1L

target_code <- bird_dates$code[
  match(target_species, bird_dates$species)
]

target_code
#> [1] "STRALU"

We then estimate phenological overlap between the focal species (synonymous to target-species) and every species in the target-group.

phenology_weights <- phenology_overlap_weights(
  target = bird_dates,
  group = bird_dates,
  target_code = target_code,
  target_id = "code",
  group_id = "code",
  target_doy = "DoY",
  group_doy = "DoY",
  type = "2",
  min_n = 5
)

phenology_weights[
  order(phenology_weights$weight, decreasing = TRUE),
]
#>          code   overlap    weight
#> STRALU STRALU 1.0000000 0.2659064
#> GLAPAS GLAPAS 0.8256341 0.2195414
#> STRURA STRURA 0.8053464 0.2141467
#> BUTBUT BUTBUT 0.6383454 0.1697401
#> CIRAER CIRAER 0.4913965 0.1306654

The returned weight values sum to one across comparison species with valid overlap estimates. Here, each target-group observation receives the weight of its species. Records are then summed within 100-m cells before KDE smoothing.

target_group_p <- merge(
  target_group,
  phenology_weights[, c("code", "weight")],
  by = "code",
  all.x = TRUE
)

target_group_p <- target_group_p[
  is.finite(target_group_p$weight) &
    !is.na(target_group_p$id100),
]

tg_weighted <- aggregate(
  list(weight = target_group_p$weight),
  by = list(id100 = target_group_p$id100),
  FUN = sum
)

idx <- match(tg_weighted$id100, points100$id)
keep <- !is.na(idx)

tg_points_weighted <- points100[idx[keep], ]
tg_points_weighted$weight <- tg_weighted$weight[keep]
phenology_bias <- kde_surface(
  x = tg_points_weighted,
  weight_field = "weight",
  sigma = 3000,
  ref = example_grid,
  normalize = "pdf",
  mask = TRUE
)

options(scipen = 999)
terra::plot(
  phenology_bias,
  main = "Phenologically weighted target-group bias"
)

Phenologically weighted target-group sampling-bias surface.

The weighted surface should be interpreted as a relative sampling-bias surface, not as an estimate of species occurrence probability. Its purpose is to describe where observations relevant to the focal species’ seasonal sampling process were more or less likely to have been collected.

Target-group weighting by seasonal and diel overlap

For taxa whose detectability varies both seasonally and through the day, seasonal overlap alone may be insufficient. torus_overlap_many() represents season and time of day as two circular dimensions and estimates overlap on a two-dimensional torus. Circular treatment is important because both annual and daily cycles wrap around their endpoints; see Mardia and Jupp (1999) for directional statistics and Ridout and Linkie (2009) for overlap estimation of diel activity patterns.

The bird dataset contains date-time observations. For this introductory example, we select the focal species with the largest number of valid date-time records and compare its seasonal and diel observation distributions with those of every species in the target group (including the focal species itself).

comparison_data <- aves_small[
  !is.na(aves_small$date_time),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

target_species_torus <- names(
  sort(table(comparison_data$species), decreasing = TRUE)
)[1]

reference_data <- comparison_data[
  comparison_data$species == target_species_torus,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

reference_data$obs_date <- as.Date(reference_data$date_time)
reference_data$obs_time <- hms::as_hms(reference_data$date_time)

comparison_data$obs_date <- as.Date(comparison_data$date_time)
comparison_data$obs_time <- hms::as_hms(comparison_data$date_time)

For speed, the example uses a coarser evaluation grid than would often be used in a final analysis.

torus_result <- torus_overlap_many(
  reference_data = reference_data,
  comparison_data = comparison_data,
  comparison_group_col = "species",
  reference_date_col = "obs_date",
  reference_time_col = "obs_time",
  comparison_date_col = "obs_date",
  comparison_time_col = "obs_time",
  reference_name = target_species_torus,
  season_bw_days = 14,
  daily_bw_hours = 1,
  date_resolution_days = 7,
  time_resolution_minutes = 60,
  min_n = 5,
  return_density = FALSE
)

torus_overlap <- torus_result$overlap
torus_overlap <- torus_overlap[
  order(torus_overlap$overlap, decreasing = TRUE),
]

head(torus_overlap, 10)
#>     reference            comparison n_reference n_comparison    overlap status
#> 4 Strix aluco           Strix aluco        3004         3004 1.00000000     OK
#> 5 Strix aluco       Strix uralensis        3004          137 0.86931899     OK
#> 3 Strix aluco Glaucidium passerinum        3004          330 0.41910228     OK
#> 2 Strix aluco    Circus aeruginosus        3004          671 0.04184691     OK
#> 1 Strix aluco           Buteo buteo        3004         2095 0.03477199     OK

The overlap coefficient ranges from zero to one for normalised densities. A large value indicates that a comparison species has a seasonal-diel observation distribution similar to the focal species.

To use these coefficients as relative species weights in a target group, they can be normalised across comparison species.

ok <- is.finite(torus_overlap$overlap)

torus_overlap$weight <- NA_real_
torus_overlap$weight[ok] <-
  torus_overlap$overlap[ok] /
  sum(torus_overlap$overlap[ok])

head(
  torus_overlap[
    order(torus_overlap$weight, decreasing = TRUE),
    c("comparison", "overlap", "weight")
  ],
  10
)
#>              comparison    overlap     weight
#> 4           Strix aluco 1.00000000 0.42282580
#> 5       Strix uralensis 0.86931899 0.36757050
#> 3 Glaucidium passerinum 0.41910228 0.17720726
#> 2    Circus aeruginosus 0.04184691 0.01769395
#> 1           Buteo buteo 0.03477199 0.01470250

These weights can be joined back to the individual observations and passed to kde_surface() in exactly the same way as the phenological weights above.

The overlap can also be visualised, when setting return_density = TRUE

torus_result <- torus_overlap_many(
  reference_data = reference_data,
  comparison_data = comparison_data,
  comparison_group_col = "species",
  reference_date_col = "obs_date",
  reference_time_col = "obs_time",
  comparison_date_col = "obs_date",
  comparison_time_col = "obs_time",
  reference_name = target_species_torus,
  season_bw_days = 14,
  daily_bw_hours = 1,
  date_resolution_days = 7,
  time_resolution_minutes = 60,
  min_n = 5,
  return_density = TRUE
)

ggplot(torus_result$density,
       aes(
         x = seasonal_position_days,
         y = decimal_hour,
         fill = comparison_density
         )
       ) +
  geom_raster() +
  facet_wrap(~ comparison) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 3)) +
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis() +
  labs(
    x = "Seasonal position (days from 1 January)",
       y = "Time of day",
       fill = "Density",
       title = "Species-specific registration activity") +
  theme_bw()


ggplot(torus_result$density,
       aes(
         x = seasonal_position_days,
         y = decimal_hour,
         fill = shared_density
         )
       ) +
  geom_raster() +
  facet_wrap(~ comparison) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 3)) +
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis() +
  labs(x = "Seasonal position (days from 1 January)",
       y = "Time of day",
       fill = "Density",
       title = paste0(
         "Registration activity overlap with ", 
         target_species_torus
         )
       ) +
  theme_bw()

Known inventory dates

Sometimes the dates of a survey or habitat inventory are known, while the species itself was not necessarily recorded during that survey. In this case, doy_kde_weights() can estimate how closely each inventory date corresponds to the seasonal registration-activity distribution of a target species.

The function estimates a circular approximation to a day-of-year KDE from the reference dates and evaluates that density at another set of dates. Circularity is approximated by periodically extending the reference observations across the seasonal boundary, which reduces boundary effects between observations near the end and beginning of the year. Bandwidth controls the degree of smoothing, as in conventional KDE (Silverman 1986).

The example below uses one bryophyte species considered to be an old-growth forest specialist and therefore specifically searched for during habitat inventories.

bryophyta_species <- names(
  sort(table(bryophyta_one$species), decreasing = TRUE)
)[1]

reference_dates <- bryophyta_one$date[
  bryophyta_one$species == bryophyta_species &
    !is.na(bryophyta_one$date)
]

inventory_keep <- !is.na(habitat_inventories$date)

inventory_weights <- doy_kde_weights(
  A_dates = reference_dates,
  B_dates = habitat_inventories$date[inventory_keep],
  scale = "percentile_A",
  bw = "nrd0"
)

weighted_inventories <- habitat_inventories[inventory_keep, ]
weighted_inventories$phenology_weight <- inventory_weights$weights

With scale = "percentile_A", weights describe how high the estimated reference density is relative to density values across the seasonal cycle. They are relative phenological correspondence scores rather than occurrence probabilities.

aggregate(
  phenology_weight ~ habitat_type,
  data = weighted_inventories,
  FUN = mean
)
#>   habitat_type phenology_weight
#> 1         dune        0.7492080
#> 2       forest        0.7281414
#> 3   freshwater        0.6848989
#> 4    grassland        0.6864115
#> 5      heather        0.0630137
#> 6         mire        0.6161949

The estimated seasonal reference curve can also be inspected directly.

plot(
  inventory_weights$density$x,
  inventory_weights$density$y,
  type = "l",
  xlab = "Day of year",
  ylab = "Estimated reference density"
)

Estimated seasonal registration-activity curve used for weighting known inventory dates.

Selecting an independent testing set

Random train-test splitting can give overly optimistic estimates of predictive performance when nearby observations are spatially dependent. Spatially structured resampling is therefore generally preferable when the intended prediction involves geographic transfer (Roberts et al. 2017).

sdmhelpers does not define the spatial blocks themselves. Instead, select_folds_by_quota() and select_joint_folds() select complete groups from fold identifiers created elsewhere. Independence therefore comes from the design of the folds, not from the selection function.

The package contains example presence records, background records, and independent spatial polygons.

pres_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(
  example_presences,
  coords = c("x", "y"),
  crs = 3059
)

bg_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(
  example_background,
  coords = c("x", "y"),
  crs = 3059
)

block_id <- setdiff(
  names(example_independent_blocks),
  attr(example_independent_blocks, "sf_column")
)[1]

pres_joined <- sf::st_join(
  pres_sf,
  example_independent_blocks[block_id],
  join = sf::st_within,
  left = TRUE
)

bg_joined <- sf::st_join(
  bg_sf,
  example_independent_blocks[block_id],
  join = sf::st_within,
  left = TRUE
)

pres_folds <- pres_joined[[block_id]]
bg_folds <- bg_joined[[block_id]]

When both presences and background should be withheld from the same spatial blocks, select_joint_folds() is convenient.

independent <- select_joint_folds(
  pres_folds = pres_folds,
  bg_folds = bg_folds,
  target_prop = 0.25,
  pres_bounds = c(0.20, 0.30),
  bg_bounds = c(0.20, 0.30),
  max_tries = 3000,
  bg_match_weight = 1,
  seed = 1,
  print_report = FALSE
)

independent$selected_fold_ids

The returned logical vectors preserve the row order of the input data and can be used directly for subsetting.

pres_test <- example_presences[independent$pres_selected_idx, ]
pres_train <- example_presences[!independent$pres_selected_idx, ]

bg_test <- example_background[independent$bg_selected_idx, ]
bg_train <- example_background[!independent$bg_selected_idx, ]

c(
  pres_train = nrow(pres_train),
  pres_test = nrow(pres_test),
  bg_train = nrow(bg_train),
  bg_test = nrow(bg_test)
)
#> pres_train  pres_test   bg_train    bg_test 
#>       2084        694      30043       9957

If only one type of observation needs to be selected, the simpler select_folds_by_quota() can be used instead.

presence_only_selection <- select_folds_by_quota(
  folds = pres_folds,
  target_prop = 0.25,
  bounds = c(0.20, 0.30),
  seed = 1,
  print_report = FALSE
)

presence_only_selection$summary$prop_selected
#> [1] 0.299964

Screening predictor variance

Predictors that are constant across all data used for model fitting cannot provide an estimable environmental response. Low variance within an individual subset, however, does not necessarily imply that a predictor is uninformative: for example, a predictor may be constant among presences but variable among background records. screen_egv_variance() therefore distinguishes the presence, background, and combined-data checks and records which checks contribute to predictor selection.

The example environmental raster contains five ecogeographical variables. The presence and background locations were split spatially into independent training and testing sets in the preceding section.

env <- terra::rast(egv_file)
env
#> class       : SpatRaster
#> size        : 650, 650, 5  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 100, 100  (x, y)
#> extent      : 455000, 520000, 280000, 345000  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : LKS-92 / Latvia TM (EPSG:3059)
#> source      : example_egv.tif
#> names       :   egv_280,   egv_293,   egv_302,   egv_385,   egv_400
#> min values  : -0.466794, -0.719917, -0.397964, -1.461203,  -0.37327
#> max values  :   3.70894,  7.054723,  8.359298,  5.206886, 11.300995

We first prepare the training and independent-testing datasets once, using the same environmental predictors. SDMtune::prepareSWD() removes locations with missing values in any supplied environmental layer. Many example records fall outside the raster’s complete-data domain; the counts below show how many observations remain after extraction. All subsequent checks, fold assignments, model fitting, and evaluation use these retained records.

training_set <- SDMtune::prepareSWD(
  species = "example_species",
  p = pres_train,
  a = bg_train,
  env = env,
  verbose = FALSE
)
#> Warning: ! 2009 locations are NA for some environmental variables and have been
#>   discarded
#> Warning: ! 28679 locations are NA for some environmental variables and have been
#>   discarded

testing_set <- SDMtune::prepareSWD(
  species = "example_species",
  p = pres_test,
  a = bg_test,
  env = env,
  verbose = FALSE
)
#> Warning: ! 613 locations are NA for some environmental
#> variables and have been discarded
#> Warning: ! 8890 locations are NA for some environmental variables and have been
#>   discarded

c(
  training_presences = sum(training_set@pa == 1),
  training_background = sum(training_set@pa == 0),
  testing_presences = sum(testing_set@pa == 1),
  testing_background = sum(testing_set@pa == 0)
)
#>  training_presences training_background   testing_presences  testing_background 
#>                  75                1364                  81                1067

For spatial cross-validation, we assign folds after the environmental-value extraction so that the fold identifiers correspond exactly to rows in the training SWD object. ENMeval::get.block() expects longitude-latitude coordinates; the projected EPSG:3059 coordinates are therefore converted to EPSG:4326 solely for constructing the folds. This does not change the predictor values stored in training_set.

as_lonlat <- function(coords) {
  pts <- sf::st_as_sf(
    coords,
    coords = c("X", "Y"),
    crs = 3059
  )
  ll <- sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_transform(pts, 4326))
  data.frame(lon = ll[, 1], lat = ll[, 2])
}

pres_idx <- training_set@pa == 1
bg_idx <- training_set@pa == 0

block_folds <- ENMeval::get.block(
  occs = as_lonlat(training_set@coords[pres_idx, , drop = FALSE]),
  bg = as_lonlat(training_set@coords[bg_idx, , drop = FALSE])
)

The screen checks presences, backgrounds, and their combination both across all training records and within each cross-validation training partition. Because bg_folds is supplied, the corresponding held-out background fold is excluded as well as the presence fold. Presence-only checks are retained as diagnostics but do not automatically remove predictors. The independent test set can also be diagnosed, while the default leakage-safe settings ensure that its values do not affect keep or remove.

variance_screen <- screen_egv_variance(
  train = training_set,
  test = testing_set,
  occ_folds = block_folds$occs.grp,
  bg_folds = block_folds$bg.grp,
  env = env,
  env_sample_n = 5000L,
  seed = 1L,
  sd_tol = 0,
  check_presences = TRUE,
  check_background = TRUE,
  check_combined = TRUE,
  presence_affects_selection = FALSE,
  include_test_bg = FALSE,
  check_test = TRUE,
  test_affects_selection = FALSE,
  verbose = FALSE
)

variance_screen$keep
#> [1] "egv_280" "egv_293" "egv_302" "egv_385" "egv_400"
variance_screen$remove
#> character(0)

A predictor is removed only if it fails at least one check marked used_for_selection = TRUE. A failed diagnostic-only check remains visible in diagnostics but does not affect predictor selection. Even though this example calculates diagnostic-only checks on the independent test, their results must not be used to revise the chosen predictor set or model. In a final analysis, it is preferable not to inspect the held-out test diagnostics until the model specification has been fixed.

head(variance_screen$diagnostics)
#>      check subset data_source      group fold used_for_selection variable
#> 1 training    all    training  presences <NA>              FALSE  egv_280
#> 2 training    all    training  presences <NA>              FALSE  egv_293
#> 3 training    all    training  presences <NA>              FALSE  egv_302
#> 4 training    all    training  presences <NA>              FALSE  egv_385
#> 5 training    all    training  presences <NA>              FALSE  egv_400
#> 6 training    all    training background <NA>               TRUE  egv_280
#>   n_finite        sd failed reason
#> 1       75 1.5562103  FALSE passed
#> 2       75 1.8404706  FALSE passed
#> 3       75 1.1651248  FALSE passed
#> 4       75 0.4201842  FALSE passed
#> 5       75 0.4363026  FALSE passed
#> 6     1364 1.5236134  FALSE passed

subset(
  variance_screen$diagnostics,
  failed & !used_for_selection,
  select = c(check, subset, group, variable, sd, reason)
)
#> [1] check    subset   group    variable sd       reason  
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

The random environmental-domain check samples raster cells independently of the observed training background locations. It does not resample the background records already contained in training_set.

A common predictor set screened across all CV partitions is convenient for this introductory example. For an unbiased assessment of a pipeline that selects predictors anew, that selection must instead be performed separately inside each CV training partition.

subset(
  variance_screen$diagnostics,
  check == "cv_training",
  select = c(
    check, subset, group, fold,
    variable, sd, failed, used_for_selection
  )
)

Fitting a small maxnet model

sdmhelpers supports rather than replaces SDM software. Here we fit a small illustrative maxnet model to the training data using only the predictors retained by the variance screen. This model is for demonstration; the cross-validation example below can be used to compare alternative feature classes and regularisation multipliers before fitting a final model.

selected_vars <- variance_screen$keep

if (!length(selected_vars)) {
  stop("No predictors passed variance screening.")
}

maxnet_model <- maxnet::maxnet(
  p = training_set@pa,
  data = training_set@data[, selected_vars, drop = FALSE],
  addsamplestobackground = TRUE
)

Following the conventional Maxent approach, presence locations not already represented in the background are additionally included as background samples during model fitting. This behaviour is enabled by addsamplestobackground = TRUE, which is also the default in maxnet.

We do not separately call SDMtune::addSamplesToBg() because maxnet handles this operation internally. Consequently, the original training_set object remains unchanged, and its presence and background records can be used consistently for subsequent evaluation and cross-validation.

Importantly, this operation uses only the training data. Independent testing presences and background records remain withheld from model fitting.

Evaluating models with TSS

The true skill statistic (TSS) is defined as

\[ \mathrm{TSS} = \mathrm{sensitivity} + \mathrm{specificity} - 1. \]

max_tss() evaluates candidate thresholds and returns the threshold that maximizes TSS, together with sensitivity and specificity. For presence-background data, background locations are not confirmed absences; thus the reported specificity is the proportion of background records classified as negative, and TSS should be interpreted as presence-background discrimination rather than classification accuracy against known absences (Allouche et al. 2006).

Critically, selecting a threshold using independent-test predictions and then reporting TSS on that same test set would yield a test-optimized estimate. Here we select the threshold using training predictions only, and then apply it unchanged to the withheld independent test. The resulting independent-test TSS is not optimized on test labels, although the threshold chosen on fitting data may be optimistic for the training sample itself.

train_p_pos <- predict(
  maxnet_model,
  newdata = training_set@data[
    training_set@pa == 1, selected_vars, drop = FALSE
  ],
  type = "cloglog"
)

train_p_bg <- predict(
  maxnet_model,
  newdata = training_set@data[
    training_set@pa == 0, selected_vars, drop = FALSE
  ],
  type = "cloglog"
)

training_tss <- max_tss(p_pos = train_p_pos, p_neg = train_p_bg)
threshold <- unname(training_tss["threshold"])
training_tss
#>         tss   threshold sensitivity specificity 
#>   0.7227370   0.1993446   0.9866667   0.7360704
test_p_pos <- predict(
  maxnet_model,
  newdata = testing_set@data[
    testing_set@pa == 1, selected_vars, drop = FALSE
  ],
  type = "cloglog"
)

test_p_bg <- predict(
  maxnet_model,
  newdata = testing_set@data[
    testing_set@pa == 0, selected_vars, drop = FALSE
  ],
  type = "cloglog"
)

independent_sensitivity <- mean(test_p_pos >= threshold)
independent_background_specificity <- mean(test_p_bg < threshold)

c(
  threshold_from_training = threshold,
  sensitivity = independent_sensitivity,
  background_specificity = independent_background_specificity,
  independent_TSS = independent_sensitivity +
    independent_background_specificity - 1
)
#> threshold_from_training             sensitivity  background_specificity 
#>               0.1993446               0.9012346               0.6269916 
#>         independent_TSS 
#>               0.5282261

The same threshold can be applied to predictions at raster cells when a binary suitability map is needed. For an independent final evaluation, the threshold and all predictor-selection and tuning decisions should be fixed before the held-out test predictions are examined.

Cross-validation TSS with ENMeval

The independent testing set created earlier is reserved for the final assessment of the fitted model. Model tuning instead uses spatial cross-validation of the training data, keeping the independent testing set out of predictor-selection and tuning decisions. Spatial resampling can reduce dependence between model calibration and validation observations when the intended prediction involves geographic transfer (Roberts et al. 2017).

ENMeval supports spatial partitions and multiple complexity settings for Maxent and maxnet models (Muscarella et al. 2014; Kass et al. 2021). We reuse the four presence and background fold assignments (block_folds) created in the predictor-screening section. These were calculated using the records remaining in training_set after environmental values were extracted, so their ordering matches the model inputs. There is no need to generate a second set of folds.

For illustration, we compare three feature-class settings (linear, L; quadratic, Q; and linear plus quadratic, LQ) and three regularisation multipliers (0.5, 1, and 2). The regularisation multiplier controls the strength of model penalisation; thus, nine candidate settings are evaluated.

Important: The predictor set used below is the one returned by screen_egv_variance() in the preceding section. It is held constant across the candidate model settings for this introductory example.

selected_vars <- variance_screen$keep

if (length(selected_vars) == 0L) {
  stop("No predictors passed variance screening.")
}

pres_idx <- training_set@pa == 1
bg_idx <- training_set@pa == 0

# The as_lonlat() helper and block_folds were defined in the preceding section.
# ENMeval receives coordinates in the first two columns, followed by predictors.
presences <- cbind(
  as_lonlat(training_set@coords[pres_idx, , drop = FALSE]),
  training_set@data[pres_idx, selected_vars, drop = FALSE]
)

background <- cbind(
  as_lonlat(training_set@coords[bg_idx, , drop = FALSE]),
  training_set@data[bg_idx, selected_vars, drop = FALSE]
)

stopifnot(
  length(block_folds$occs.grp) == nrow(presences),
  length(block_folds$bg.grp) == nrow(background)
)

Following the conventional Maxent approach, occurrence locations are additionally included among the background samples used for model fitting by setting addsamplestobackground = TRUE. This behavior is the default in both maxnet and ENMeval’s Maxnet implementation. During spatial cross-validation, only the training data for each partition should contribute to model fitting, while validation presences and backgrounds remain withheld for evaluation. The option validation.bg = "partition" additionally restricts validation comparisons to the background records assigned to the corresponding validation partition.

enmeval_result <- ENMeval::ENMevaluate(
  occs = presences,
  bg = background,
  algorithm = "maxnet",
  partitions = "user",
  user.grp = list(
    occs.grp = block_folds$occs.grp,
    bg.grp = block_folds$bg.grp
  ),
  tune.args = list(
    fc = c("L", "Q", "LQ"),
    rm = c(0.5, 1, 2)
  ),
  other.settings = list(
    validation.bg = "partition",
    addsamplestobackground = TRUE
  ),
  user.eval = tss_user_eval
)
#>   |                                                                              |                                                                      |   0%  |                                                                              |========                                                              |  11%  |                                                                              |================                                                      |  22%  |                                                                              |=======================                                               |  33%  |                                                                              |===============================                                       |  44%  |                                                                              |=======================================                               |  56%  |                                                                              |===============================================                       |  67%  |                                                                              |======================================================                |  78%  |                                                                              |==============================================================        |  89%  |                                                                              |======================================================================| 100%

The user.eval = tss_user_eval argument adds the package’s custom TSS calculations. For each candidate model and cross-validation fold, ENMeval supplies predictions for training and validation occurrences and background records. tss_user_eval() applies max_tss() separately to the training and validation predictions. Its fold-level output includes maximum validation TSS (tss.val), the corresponding validation threshold (thr.val), sensitivity (sens.val), background-based specificity (spec.val), and maximum training TSS (tss.train).

In presence-background models, background locations are not confirmed absences. Consequently, spec.val is the proportion of background predictions below the selected threshold, not specificity estimated using verified absences.

Interpretation of threshold optimisation. Since thr.val is selected to maximise TSS on the same validation observations used to calculate tss.val, validation TSS is optimised for that fold. The spatial validation records were withheld from model fitting, but not from threshold selection. Accordingly, these TSS values can help compare candidate settings, but should not be presented as fully independent estimates of the performance of a preselected classification threshold. For a final independent threshold-based assessment, select the threshold without reference to the independent test outcomes and apply it unchanged to that test set, as described in the preceding evaluation section.

The model-level results aggregate values across folds. A compact table is more useful in an introductory vignette than printing every available statistic:

cv_results <- ENMeval::eval.results(enmeval_result)

knitr::kable(
  cv_results[, c(
    "fc", "rm", "auc.val.avg",
    "tss.val.avg", "tss.val.sd",
    "AICc", "delta.AICc"
  )],
  digits = 3
)
fc rm auc.val.avg tss.val.avg tss.val.sd AICc delta.AICc
L 0.5 0.825 0.579 0.098 938.411 12.058
Q 0.5 0.822 0.603 0.115 962.050 35.697
LQ 0.5 0.853 0.614 0.107 930.219 3.866
L 1.0 0.829 0.581 0.092 938.451 12.097
Q 1.0 0.838 0.614 0.127 962.161 35.808
LQ 1.0 0.851 0.603 0.102 931.310 4.956

Q 2.0 0.837 0.612 0.132 962.567 36.214
LQ 2.0 0.846 0.595 0.100 926.353 0.000

Here, the Continuous Boyce Index (CBI) is available only when the optional ecospat dependency is installed. Moreover, because the example passes extracted environmental values rather than a full environmental raster to ENMevaluate(), its AICc calculation uses the supplied background predictions as an approximation to the environmental domain. Both points matter when interpreting or comparing these statistics.

Fold-specific statistics can also be inspected; the fold column identifies the validation partition:

cv_folds <- ENMeval::eval.results.partitions(enmeval_result)

knitr::kable(
  head(cv_folds[, c(
    "tune.args", "fold", "auc.val",
    "tss.val", "thr.val", "tss.train"
  )], 12),
  digits = 3
)
tune.args fold auc.val tss.val thr.val tss.train
fc.L_rm.0.5 1 0.809 0.573 0.412 0.658
fc.L_rm.0.5 2 0.754 0.497 0.082 0.652
fc.L_rm.0.5 3 0.816 0.527 0.711 0.643
fc.L_rm.0.5 4 0.920 0.718 0.371 0.592
fc.Q_rm.0.5 1 0.743 0.521 0.286 0.666
fc.Q_rm.0.5 2 0.828 0.673 0.164 0.666
fc.Q_rm.0.5 3 0.801 0.490 0.664 0.712

fc.LQ_rm.0.5 1 0.796 0.563 0.436 0.766
fc.LQ_rm.0.5 2 0.845 0.597 0.039 0.652
fc.LQ_rm.0.5 3 0.839 0.527 0.668 0.741
fc.LQ_rm.0.5 4 0.932 0.769 0.207 0.695

Cross-validation helps choose model settings using the training dataset. The final model can then be fitted using the selected predictors and model settings and evaluated once with the withheld independent test set. In a fully nested evaluation of the complete modelling procedure, predictor screening and other data-dependent preprocessing would also be repeated within each cross-validation training fold rather than performed once on all training records.

Final model selection and independent testing

After evaluating alternative model settings using spatial cross-validation, the preferred model can be selected from the ENMevaluation object. ENMeval stores models fitted using the complete training dataset for each combination of feature classes and regularisation multipliers. Consequently, there is no need to fit the selected model again manually.

The independent testing dataset remains withheld from predictor screening decisions, model tuning, and fitting.

Selecting the preferred model

For this introductory example, we select the model with the lowest corrected Akaike Information Criterion (AICc). Other selection strategies may also consider cross-validation performance or a combination of criteria.

cv_results <- ENMeval::eval.results(enmeval_result)

valid_models <- which(is.finite(cv_results$AICc))

if (!length(valid_models)) {
  stop("No candidate model has a finite AICc.")
}

best_idx <- valid_models[
  which.min(cv_results$AICc[valid_models])
]

best_settings <- cv_results[best_idx, , drop = FALSE]

best_settings[, c(
  "fc", "rm", "tune.args",
  "AICc", "delta.AICc",
  "auc.val.avg", "tss.val.avg"
)]
#>   fc rm  tune.args     AICc delta.AICc auc.val.avg tss.val.avg
#> 9 LQ  2 fc.LQ_rm.2 926.3533          0   0.8459701   0.5950956

Extracting the selected model

The tune.args column identifies each candidate model within the list returned by ENMeval::eval.models(). We use this identifier to extract the model fitted with the complete training dataset.

best_model_id <- as.character(
  best_settings$tune.args[1]
)

fitted_models <- ENMeval::eval.models(enmeval_result)

final_model <- fitted_models[[best_model_id]]

if (is.null(final_model)) {
  stop("Selected model was not found in enmeval_result.")
}

stopifnot(inherits(final_model, "maxnet"))

The resulting final_model retains the feature classes, regularisation multiplier, and background convention used during ENMeval fitting. No independent testing observations have contributed to this model.

Selecting a classification threshold

To evaluate threshold-based predictive performance, we first determine the classification threshold using training predictions only.

Here, max_tss() identifies the threshold maximising TSS between training presences and background records. This threshold will subsequently be applied unchanged to the independent testing data.

selected_vars <- variance_screen$keep

train_x <- training_set@data[
  , selected_vars, drop = FALSE
]

train_y <- training_set@pa

train_predictions <- predict(
  final_model,
  newdata = train_x,
  type = "cloglog"
)

train_tss <- max_tss(
  p_pos = train_predictions[train_y == 1],
  p_neg = train_predictions[train_y == 0]
)

threshold <- unname(train_tss["threshold"])

train_tss
#>         tss   threshold sensitivity specificity 
#>   0.6778788   0.1423901   0.9733333   0.7045455

Although this threshold is optimised on the training data, it is selected without consulting the independent testing observations. Consequently, its application to the independent dataset provides an assessment of performance at a previously determined threshold.

Independent testing

The selected model is now applied to the independently withheld presence and background records. Only predictors used during model fitting are included in the prediction dataset.

test_x <- testing_set@data[
  , selected_vars, drop = FALSE
]

test_y <- testing_set@pa

# Apply ENMeval's clamping convention if enabled
if (isTRUE(enmeval_result@doClamp)) {
  test_x <- ENMeval::clamp.vars(
    orig.vals = test_x,
    ref.vals = train_x,
    left = enmeval_result@clamp.directions$left,
    right = enmeval_result@clamp.directions$right
  )
}

test_predictions <- predict(
  final_model,
  newdata = test_x,
  type = "cloglog"
)

test_pos <- test_predictions[test_y == 1]
test_bg <- test_predictions[test_y == 0]

test_sensitivity <- mean(test_pos >= threshold)
test_specificity <- mean(test_bg < threshold)

independent_tss <-
  test_sensitivity + test_specificity - 1

independent_results <- data.frame(
  model = best_model_id,
  n_presences = length(test_pos),
  n_background = length(test_bg),
  threshold = threshold,
  sensitivity = test_sensitivity,
  background_specificity = test_specificity,
  TSS = independent_tss
)

knitr::kable(
  independent_results,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Independent testing results for the selected Maxnet model."
)
Independent testing results for the selected Maxnet model.
model n_presences n_background threshold sensitivity background_specificity TSS
fc.LQ_rm.2 81 1067 0.142 0.963 0.55 0.513

Sensitivity represents the proportion of independently withheld presences classified as suitable, whereas background-based specificity represents the proportion of withheld background records classified as unsuitable.

Because background locations are not confirmed absences, TSS should be interpreted as a measure of discrimination between presences and background rather than conventional presence-absence classification accuracy.

The classification threshold was selected using the training dataset and was not re-optimised on the independent testing data. Furthermore, neither the model settings nor the predictor set were modified after examining the independent testing results.

This provides an independent assessment of the completed modelling procedure at a preselected classification threshold.
